text: The storage account module you wrote was small, a dozen lines total. Some patterns, like a production VPC with public and private subnets and NAT gateways, run hundreds of lines and are easy to get wrong. For those, you rarely write your own module — the Terraform Registry hosts thousands of published, versioned modules that Northbridge Retail's cloud team can pull in instead of building from scratch.

A registry module's source isn't a filesystem path at all, it's an address shaped like namespace slash name slash provider — terraform-aws-modules slash vpc slash aws, with no leading dot slash anywhere. Pass it a name, a CIDR block, a couple of availability zones, and subnet lists, and Northbridge Retail gets a production-shaped VPC from twenty lines of configuration instead of hand-writing every subnet and route table block.

Registry modules get downloaded during terraform init, the exact same step that resolves a local module's source and installs provider plugins. You'll see it listed right there in the output, downloading from registry.terraform.io into a dot terraform modules folder before any plan can actually run against it.

Once it's downloaded, a registry module behaves exactly like one you wrote by hand yourself. Its documented outputs — here, a list of private subnet IDs the module exposes — get read with the same module dot name dot output syntax you already know, feeding straight into an aws_instance resource's subnet_id argument.

Before adopting a registry module for anything real, read its documentation page and check how actively it's maintained — it's still someone else's code, running directly against Northbridge Retail's AWS account. Next lesson covers pinning its version properly, plus the standard folder structure every module should follow, published or your own.
